narrative:
The model estimated a 36% chance that you would be a bad credit risk. Under the bank’s current cutoff, that was still too high, so your loan was denied. This does not mean repayment is certain to fail; it means the bank judged the risk above what it can accept for this application.

The most influential factor was the short requested credit term: you asked for 8 months, while approved applicants average about 19 months. That shorter exposure actually worked in your favor, pushing the decision toward good credit. The second factor was your checking account status. Your account is below zero, whereas most approved applicants either have no checking account or a positive balance; this was the strongest factor pushing toward bad credit. The third factor was your credit history. It is listed as critical/other credits, a category shared by about one third of approved applicants, and in your case it contributed slightly toward good credit rather than driving the rejection.

To improve your chances, focus on bringing your checking account out of the negative and keeping a stable non-negative balance. Ask the bank whether additional documentation, a guarantor or co-applicant, or a later application after your account status improves could change the decision. You may also request a manual review if you believe any account or credit-history information is inaccurate.
